beats: A ship drifted empty across the Atlantic, with its lifeboat gone.
This is the Mary Celeste, 1872. Ten people, including a two-year-old girl, simply gone.
No fight. Their belongings untouched. Six months of food still on board.
Only one thing was missing: the lifeboat. They left in a hurry.
Toxic fumes? A waterspout? A panic that turned deadly? No one knows.
Not one of them was ever seen again. Weeks later, their empty ship was still out there, because
Nine hikers fled their tent barefoot into a frozen night.
Russia, 1959. Minus twenty-five degrees. Some were found a kilometre away, without shoes.
Some had crushed skulls and ribs, but almost no outside wounds.
People blamed avalanches, secret weapons, even something unexplained.
In 2021, scientists said a small slab avalanche could explain the injuries.
But nine experts, fleeing into certain death? What scared them so much that
Over one hundred colonists vanished, leaving one carved word.
Roanoke, 1587. Their governor sailed to England for supplies, leaving his newborn granddaughter behind.
War trapped him there for three years.
When he returned, the settlement was empty. No bodies. No graves.
Just one word on a post: Croatoan, the name of a nearby island.
A storm stopped him from ever searching it. To this day, nobody knows why
A six-hundred-year-old book still has no readable language.
The Voynich Manuscript. Two hundred and forty pages in a script that matches no known language.
Plants that do not exist. Strange star maps. Tiny bathing figures.
Carbon dating proves it is from the early fourteen hundreds. Not a modern fake.
The best codebreakers of both world wars tried. Every one of them failed.
A lost language, or a brilliant hoax? It sits at Yale today, because
Three lighthouse keepers vanished; one coat stayed behind.
Scotland, December 1900. The Flannan Isles light went dark.
Inside, the lamp was clean. Beds made. Nothing out of place.
Outside, iron railings were twisted, equipment ripped away by the sea.
A giant wave, they said. But why were all three outside at once, in winter?
No bodies were ever found. And the strangest clue of all is still this:
A dead man had no labels, no name, and a secret code.
Adelaide, 1948. No wallet. No name. No cause of death.
In a hidden pocket, two words: Tamam Shud. It means, it is ended.
They were torn from a book of Persian poetry. Inside that book, a code nobody has cracked.
In 2022, DNA suggested his name was Carl Webb.
But who killed him, and what does the code say? It all began when
Something exploded over Siberia, a thousand times Hiroshima, and left no crater.
June 1908. Eighty million trees flattened in an instant.
People sixty kilometres away were thrown off their feet. The night sky glowed over Europe.
Scientists arrived years later expecting a giant meteorite. They found nothing.
Most think a space rock burst in the air, kilometres above the ground.
Over a city, it would have erased it. Could it happen again? Remember,
Divers found a computer in a shipwreck, and it was two thousand years old.
X-rays revealed more than thirty precise bronze gears hidden inside the rock.
Turn its handle, and it predicted eclipses, moon phases, even the Olympic Games.
Nothing this complex appears again for over a thousand years.
Who built it? And how was that knowledge simply lost?
We only know because, in 1901,
A man hijacked a plane, jumped into the night with the cash, and vanished.
1971. He called himself Dan Cooper, and calmly handed a flight attendant a note: I have a bomb.
He demanded two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes.
Over the forests of Washington, he opened the rear stairs and leapt into the rain.
Years later, a boy found some of the cash buried by a river.
Did he die, or get away with it? The FBI still can't say, because
Five Navy bombers vanished, then the plane sent to find them vanished too.
December 1945, off Florida. How did fourteen airmen and a rescue plane disappear?
His compasses failed, the leader radioed, and he thought he was over the Florida Keys.
But they were likely near the Bahamas, so his corrections led them farther out to sea.
Proven: five bombers and a rescue plane were lost. Probable: the bombers ditched, out of fuel. Unknown: where they sank.
The Triangle got the legend; the evidence points to a wrong guess over a winter sea.
The drawings seem made for the sky, yet their makers stood on the ground.
Why carve huge figures and lines into Peru’s desert?
People removed dark stones, exposing lighter soil to form animals, shapes, and long paths.
New research suggests small figures and giant networks served different audiences.
Proven: the geoglyphs date broadly from 500 BC to AD 500. Probable: ritual uses fit. Unknown: one complete purpose.
The aerial view may be ours; the builders may have designed a landscape to walk.
An island left a script, then lost everyone who could read it.
Is Easter Island's rongorongo real writing, and could it ever be read?
In the 1860s, missionaries found wooden tablets covered in tiny carved glyphs.
But slave raids and disease had just devastated the island; its readers were gone.
Proven: about two dozen objects survive, one on wood older than European contact. Probable: it was a real script. Unknown: its meaning.
The writing survived on wood; what vanished were the people who could hear it.
Eight people went to sleep in one Iowa house; none woke up.
Who killed the Moore family and two young guests in Villisca in 1912?
The killer used the family's own axe, then covered the mirrors and faces.
But hundreds of townspeople walked through the house before police sealed it.
Proven: eight were killed and no one was convicted. Probable: the killer hid inside before they returned. Unknown: who it was.
They slept in a house where the killer was probably already waiting.
A boat carrying twenty-five people was found drifting, and everyone was gone.
October 1955, South Pacific. Where did the Joyita's passengers and crew go?
Five weeks later she was found half sunk, cargo gone, life rafts missing.
But cork lining kept her afloat; a broken pipe had flooded her slowly.
Proven: the radio was set to the distress channel. Probable: they abandoned her, fearing she would sink. Unknown: what happened next.
The boat that frightened them off was the one thing that refused to sink.
A millionaire banked a fortune, then vanished without touching a cent.
What happened to Toronto theatre owner Ambrose Small in December 1919?
He sold his theatres, deposited a one million dollar cheque, and left his office.
Soon after, his secretary vanished too, with bonds stolen from Small.
Proven: Small was never seen again, and the secretary was jailed for theft, not murder. Probable: foul play. Unknown: who and why.
The money stayed in the bank; the man who earned it is the only thing missing.
A woman started dancing in the street, and for days she could not stop.
Strasbourg, 1518. Within weeks, dozens joined her. What made them dance?
Doctors called it an illness of hot blood, and the cure was more dancing. So the city hired musicians.
But with music, the dancers multiplied. A sickness of the body does not spread by watching.
Proven: records describe the outbreak. Probable: mass panic, in hungry people who feared a dancing curse. Unknown: the exact cause.
And the musicians hired to cure it probably made the fire burn hotter.
Two well-dressed men were found dead on a hill, wearing lead eye masks.
Brazil, 1966. Two electronics technicians, and no wounds. What killed them?
A note beside them said: take the capsules, then wait for the signal. Maybe a drug.
But no capsules were found, and doctors could not find a cause of death.
Proven: the men, the masks and the note were real. Probable: a ritual or experiment went wrong. Unknown: what killed them.
Their death is certain, and so is their belief. Only the signal they waited for is missing.
Six people were murdered on a farm, but someone stayed there for days.
Bavaria, 1922. Who killed the family at Hinterkaifeck?
Before the murders, the farmer saw footprints in the snow leading in, and none leading out. Maybe someone was hiding.
One thing did not fit a robbery: the family's money was left untouched.
Proven: after the killings, someone fed the animals and smoke rose from the chimney. Probable: the killer hid in the house. Unknown: who.
Those footprints went only one way, perhaps because their owner never meant to leave.
A famous pilot sounded close by on the radio, yet nobody saw her.
1937. Amelia Earhart hunted for a tiny Pacific island. Why didn't she reach it?
She radioed: we must be on you, but cannot see you, and gas is running low.
The ship heard her clearly; she could not hear the ship.
Proven: the plane vanished near Howland Island. Probable: it ran out of fuel and went down at sea. Unknown: where it lies.
That close voice was not rescue; it was someone beside her goal, unable to see it.
A killer mailed coded letters to newspapers. One took fifty-one years to crack.
California, late 1960s. He called himself the Zodiac. Who was he?
A couple cracked his first code within days. Maybe it would reveal his name.
But in that code, he wrote he would not give his name. The second, solved in 2020, had none either.
Proven: at least five murders. Probable: the letters came from the killer. Unknown: his identity.
His long codes were opened; the shortest one, which might hold his name, is still locked.
London's most famous killer has a name, but nobody knows who owned it.
1888, Whitechapel. Five women were murdered. Who did it?
Police received hundreds of letters; one was signed Jack the Ripper. Maybe the killer wrote it.
But most letters were hoaxes, and that famous one was probably written by a journalist.
Proven: the murders happened. Probable: one man killed all five. Unknown: who he was; a DNA claim on a shawl is disputed.
So the most famous part of the case may not be the killer's work, but a newspaper's.
A man in a rubber mask hijacked live TV, and was never caught.
Chicago, 1987. In the middle of a broadcast, a masked face took over. Who was he?
This needed equipment and know-how. Maybe someone who knew television from the inside.
Two hours later, he hit a second station. This was no accident; it was a plan.
Proven: a stronger signal overpowered the station links. Probable: people with broadcast skills. Unknown: who they were.
We know how he did it, just not who he was. And he never came back.
